extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, chymists and experimental chemists (readers assessing chymical doctrines and experiments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging whether substances and purported 'principles' obtained by chymical operations (distillation, extraction) are truly elementary, and for assessing the adequacy of experimental and theoretical claims about elemental composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not name distillation products as elements without proof of simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Those distinct Substances which Chymists obtain from mixt Bodies by Vulgar Distillation are not to be presumed pure, simple, or properly called Elements or Principles merely because they are separable by fire or menstruums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle insists that separated substances often remain 'mixt Bodies' and that further analysis (e.g., further distillation, resolution) is required before calling them elementary. Example/anti-pattern: calling the oil or tincture an 'element' because it is inflammable or coloured is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require successful, exacting experiments before assent
rubrics_metrics.description: Withhold belief from chymists' promises until their Experiments exact it; do not accept speculative claims without exact experimental demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author says promises are easily made and less easily made good; one must insist on experimental demonstration and exactness. Anti-pattern: accepting a practitioner's claim on hearsay or authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear, unambiguous terminology over traditional metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ambiguous or abused words (e.g., 'mercury') and prefer clearer appellations (e.g., 'spirit') when the traditional name misleads or is used inconsistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle recommends substituting clearer familiar names to avoid confusion. Example: replacing 'Mercury' with 'Spirit' to reduce ambiguity; anti-pattern: leaving mystical or metaphorical epithets unexamined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not define principles by a single sensible quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles should not be defined solely by one property such as volatility, taste, or inflammability, because those properties can be shared by different underlying substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that volatility, taste, or inflammability may be present in mixtures and so cannot serve as a decisive definition. Anti-pattern: defining 'mercury' as simply whatever is volatile upon calcination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring identity from resemblance in one quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity in one general quality (e.g., fluidity, dryness, volatility) is a gross basis for concluding two substances are the same in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple qualities (actions on senses, chemical behaviour, further resolution) rather than single shared traits. Example: many different calxes are dry and fixed but differ fundamentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test simplicity by further analysis (e.g., redistillation, resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge whether an extracted substance is truly simple, submit it to further operations — distillation, dissolution, or other analyses — to see whether it resolves into differing substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle gives examples where tinctures drawn by spirit of wine yield multiple substances upon subsequent distillation. Anti-pattern: stopping at a first extraction and declaring elemental status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of contamination from the separatory agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that solvents and 'menstruums' (e.g., spirit of wine) may dissolve and carry away mixtures of ingredients rather than a single elementary ingredient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes spirit of wine can dissolve resinous, saline, and mercurial parts together; therefore separations performed by other bodies may produce mixed extracts. Ensure separation method itself is not producing artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume the fire is the adequate and universal analyzer
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not presuppose that fire, as an analyzer, reveals the true, pre-existing components of all concretes; the fire may create new arrangements and emergent qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle argues the fire can change texture and motion of small parts and endow new qualities (e.g., flame) without proving pre-existence of those parts. The claim that fire simply exposes pre-existing 'elements' needs independent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require generality across classes before asserting a fixed number of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: If one asserts a universal scheme (e.g., three or five principles), that scheme should hold across different kingdoms (vegetable, animal, mineral) and not be inferred from a subset (e.g., easily distilled vegetable bodies) alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle points out that an account based on vegetation/animals may not apply to minerals like gold and silver; a universal account must be evidenced across such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand internal consistency in theoretical doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorist's doctrine (e.g., Paracelsus' tria prima) should be coherent and consistent across writings; inconsistent or self-contradictory accounts weaken the doctrine's authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle cites Paracelsus as writing inconsistently about his principles; one should prefer consistent descriptions and clear definitions rather than variable metaphors or encomia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and reconcile counterexamples and divergent properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming a principle has particular properties (acidic, saline, inflammable), address cases where purported instances differ (e.g., spirits that are acidic versus spirits that are saline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists many spirits with divergent tastes and behaviours; a solid claim must account for such diversity rather than ignore it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple experimental qualities (taste, inflammability, solubility, colour, physiological action) to distinguish substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify and judge substances using a suite of sensible and experimental properties rather than relying on a single characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle repeatedly refers to taste, inflammability, fixity, solubility, colour, and medicinal effects as discriminating features; combine these observations to assess sameness or difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of naming-based authority (patronage of a name does not imply reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that practitioners give distinct virtues or names (e.g., 'Tincture of Gold', 'Tincture of Antimony') does not establish that the named extracts are true elementary sulphurs or salts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle warns that chymists may 'allow themselves a License to abuse Words' and that names and asserted specific virtues are insufficient proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge method-dependence of separations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that different separation procedures (distillation, solution by spirit of wine, rainwater leaching) yield different results; the method shapes what is obtained and so conclusions about elemental structure must account for method-dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: vitriol soaked by rain produces a coagulable substance; spirit of wine extracts different resins and tinctures. Thus reproducible, method-controlled experiments are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer primitiveness from transformability (e.g., oil to flame)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a substance can be converted (by fire or other means) into something else (e.g., oil into flame), that transformability undermines claims that it is a primitive, incorruptible body unless reversible demonstration is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boyle asks whether anyone has caught and recollected the dissipated parts of flame back into oil; inability to reverse transformations casts doubt on primogenial status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate experimental evidence from speculative explanatory reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between empirical demonstrations (experiments) and speculative philosophical reasons; prioritize the former when evaluating claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carneades (Boyle's interlocutor) limits his inquiry to examining experiments rather than the speculative reasons given to justify hypothesized element counts. Anti-pattern: treating speculative rationales as evidence.
